subject: Proposed fix for uneven spacing when using coord_polar

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Proposed fix for uneven spacing when using coord_polar
parts:
Hi everyone - I have a proposed fix for a problem with uneven angular spacing when using coord_polar, and Hadley suggested I ask the list for some feedback. If you're a frequent user of coord_polar, perhaps you can offer some insights.

The problem is that when using bars with width < 1, the spacing is uneven:

dat <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:3], y=4)
# Bad
# A and C boxes touch - angle AC is smaller than AB and BC
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_bar() + coord_polar()


There's more information about the problem and possible solution here:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/473


Thanks!
-Winston

parts:
If you use expand=c(0,0), you end up with the same picture I attached. For example, try this:

# Not enough space
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_bar() +

coord_polar(expand=T) + scale_x_discrete(expand=c(0, 0))

# Too much space -- default is c(0,0.6)
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_bar() +

coord_polar(expand=T) + scale_x_discrete()

# Just right
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_bar() +

coord_polar(expand=T) + scale_x_discrete(expand=c(0, 0.5))

The expand values apparently start from the center of each x, in this case "A", "B", and "C". The corresponding numeric x values are 1, 2, and 3. It needs to go from 0.5 to 3.5 to have equal spacing.

-Winston

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Proposed fix for uneven spacing when using coord_polar
parts:
I think that in general, there are two possible things that someone might want:
- merge the first and last. (This is possible only for zero-width geoms like geom_point)
- do not merge the first and last, and have equal angle spacing

The way you do these things is slightly different for discrete and continuous scales. In the examples below, I think D1, D2, C1, and C3 are good. I can't think of any case where someone would want to use C2.


dat <- data.frame(x=1:3, y=4)

# x is discrete
pd <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=as.factor(x), y=y)) + geom_point() +
  coord_polar(expand=T)

# D1: With no expansion, 1 and 3 are merged
pd + scale_x_discrete(expand=c(0, 0))

# D2: With expansion, 1 and 3 are separate
pd + scale_x_discrete(expand=c(0, 0.5))


# x is continuous
pc <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + coord_polar(expand=T)

# C1: With no expansion, 1 and 3 are merged
pc + scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0, 0))

# C2: With expansion, 1 and 3 are separate, but intermediate breaks are not present
pc + scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0, 0.5))

# C3: With no expansion and manual limits, the intermediate breaks are present
#  (This one is also rotated relative to the others, but that can be adjusted)
pc + scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0, 0), limits=c(0, 3))


I think you're right that a default of c(0,0) makes sense for continuous theta.

With a discrete theta, I think the choice that users face is simple: merge the first and last values, or do not merge. (Again merging isn't possible with geoms like geom_bar, that have non-zero width).

With a continuous theta, it's a little more complicated. They can merge the first and last values. Or they can not merge the first and last, but if so, then they need to specify the limits for theta (as in C3).

-Winston

On Sun, Apr 8, 2012 at 12:15 AM, Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com> wrote:

I mean that if the scale is continuous, expand = c(0, 0) would be better.
I'm not sure which is best option though.

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Proposed fix for uneven spacing when using coord_polar
parts:
OK, so this seems like a reasonable set of options:

For discrete theta: Always use expand=c(0,0.5) so that items are not merged and have equal spacing. (This is D2 from my earlier message.)

For continuous theta: Always use expand=c(0,0) so that low and high values are merged (C1). If the user wants to NOT merge the low and high values, they can specify wider limits (C3).


My opinion is that these settings should always be used with coord_polar -- they shouldn't have to do something complicated like:
# For discrete x:
coord_polar(expand=TRUE) + scale_x_discrete(expand=c(0,0.5))

# For continuous x:
coord_polar(expand=FALSE)
# or:
coord_polar(expand=TRUE) + scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0))


They should be able to just use coord_polar() without having to set those expand arguments. I can't think of any reason why someone would want to use different values for expand. Does this sound reasonable?

-Winston

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Proposed fix for uneven spacing when using coord_polar
parts:
I'm attempting to change the default expand values to NA and have made some progress, but there are still some issues that are hard to deal with. (If we decide to go with waiver(), that shouldn't be a difficult modification.)

The problem is that the scale_dimension() function is called in many places -- sometimes before the coord functions, like coord_train(), are applied, and sometimes after.

The way I've done it is by modifying coord_train() to set default expand values, if the expand values are NA. When scale_dimension() is called after coord_train(), this is fine. However, when scale_dimension() is called *before* coord_train(), it's problematic. at this point, the expand values are c(NA, NA), and when scale_dimension sees this, instead of returning the actual range, it returns c(NA, NA).

My understanding is that, for those cases of scale_dimension() that are called before coord_train(), it is impossible to use the expand values provided by the coord. Suggestions on dealing with this? I could set it so that when scale_dimension() encounters NA expand values, it will simply use 0.

This may change the behavior of some things, though. For example, with a geom_histogram, the default binwidth is 1/30 of the range. With the current code in the master branch, this range includes the expansion. If I make the change, then this range used for the binwidth calculation will NOT include the expansion, but the range of the plot will include the expansion.


Here are the changes I've made:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/pull/473/files

Here are the scale_dimension functions for discrete and continuous:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/blob/master/R/scale-.r#L248

-Winston

I think this will require some changes to how the scale_ functions are organized. scale_dimension presently calls scale_limits(), as shown here (I've modified it to use default value of 0 for expand, if expand==NA):

scale_dimension.continuous  <- function(scale, expand = scale$expand) {
  expand_range(scale_limits(scale),
    ifelse(is.na(expand[1]), 0, expand[1]),
    ifelse(is.na(expand[2]), 0, expand[2]))
}


The scale_breaks function also calls scale_limits():

scale_breaks.continuous <- function(scale, limits = scale_limits(scale)) {
  [code here]...
}


And here's the definition of scale_limits():

scale_limits.default <- function(scale) {  
  scale$limits %||% scale$range$range
}


One potential solution is to change scale_breaks() to use scale_dimension instead of scale_limits:

scale_breaks.continuous <- function(scale, limits = scale_dimension(scale)) {
  [code here]...
}

Is this OK? I don't know this part of the code very well.

-Winston

At the moment scale_breaks is called by coord and guide.
So, the caller know the expand of coord.

In sum, the limits-breaks relevant functions are

UseMethod("scale_limits")
UseMethod("scale_dimension")

UseMethod("scale_breaks")
UseMethod("scale_breaks_minor")
UseMethod("scale_labels")

the last three is called only by the guides/coords.

scale_limits is the limits of values.
if stats are calculated by using the scale_limits, scale_dimension
will be also called only be guide/coord.

scale_dimension <- function(scale, expand = NULL) {
if (is.waive(scale$expand)) ex <- expand
else ex <- scale$expand
expand_range(scale_limits(scale), ex[1], ex[2])
}

coords call this like:

scale_dimension(scale, coord_expand(coord))

And finally, here again, I would suggest that NA shouldn't be used for
the flag for, e.g., out-of-range value or undefined value. NA has
special meaning.

But maybe, if stats don't use the expanded limits, scale may not be
care about expansion...

kohske

used by the stats, it's called with expand = c(0, 0).

One of the consequences of this is that now when you use a histogram with the default binwidth (1/30 range), there is always a separate bin that contains the maximum value.

For example, if you run this code with the modified code, you get a right-most bin with just the largest item in dat$x:
set.seed(121); dat <- data.frame(x=runif(1000))
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x)) + geom_histogram()

This didn't happen before, because binwidth was 1/30 of the expanded range, which is slightly larger than the data range.

So if we make this change, then we should probably change the default binwidth for stat_bin.

-Winston

>> range, which is slightly larger than the data range.
>>
>> So if we make this change, then we should probably change the default
>> binwidth for stat_bin.

This may be a floating point issue, in which case we could make the
binwidth range / 30 + range * 1e-3 or something.

I think it's not a FP issue -- it happens because the bins are closed on one side and open on the other, as in [min, max). Suppose, for example, you have data that has a range of 0 to 300, and use the default binwidth of 1/30 * (300 - 0), which is 10. Then have the following bins:
[0, 10)
[10, 20)
...
[290, 300)
[300, 310)

The last bin is needed to capture the data point(s) with value 300.

-Winston

At the moment scale_breaks is called by coord and guide.
So, the caller know the expand of coord.

In sum, the limits-breaks relevant functions are

UseMethod("scale_limits")
UseMethod("scale_dimension")

UseMethod("scale_breaks")
UseMethod("scale_breaks_minor")
UseMethod("scale_labels")

the last three is called only by the guides/coords.

scale_limits is the limits of values.
if stats are calculated by using the scale_limits, scale_dimension
will be also called only be guide/coord.

scale_dimension <- function(scale, expand = NULL) {
 if (is.waive(scale$expand)) ex <- expand
 else ex <- scale$expand
 expand_range(scale_limits(scale), ex[1], ex[2])
}

coords call this like:

scale_dimension(scale, coord_expand(coord))

And finally, here again, I would suggest that NA shouldn't be used for
the flag for, e.g., out-of-range value or undefined value. NA has
special meaning.

But maybe, if stats don't use the expanded limits, scale may not be
care about expansion...
